sourceCheck: Pinned September 2025: the versions index still lists it as Latest Release, dated 2025-09-03, and the edition heading reads September 2025 Edition. GitHub shows publication on 2025-09-04 at 06:52 UTC. The index lists a newer prerelease working draft dated 2026-09-28. PR #1244, September2026 Edition & Changelog, remains open and unmerged, with six approvals; the September2026 URL did not return a readable edition. The release and September2025 changelog confirm OneOf input objects and isOneOf; schema coordinates; descriptions on operations, fragments and variable definitions; argument/input-field deprecation and associated introspection filtering; non-null deprecated reason; subscription-root skip/include restrictions; Operation Type Existence; implementing-field deprecation constraints; mandatory String serialization for ID; expanded Unicode escapes; execution-error terminology; request extensions; clarified execution/request-error results and ignoring additional response entries; stricter schema-definition omission conditions; recommended introspection source order; and stricter error paths. October2021 was checked for the earlier wording. The Current Working Draft and pending changelog contain empty composite selection sets, directives on directive definitions, directive extensions and deprecation, directives(includeDeprecated:), OneOf inhabitability validation, revised fragment descriptions, unique-error-path wording and the Appendix D includeDeprecated fix. These changes are excluded. GraphQL over HTTP remains Current Working Draft; its versions index lists only the 2026-09-28 prerelease. All 14 supplied Learn/spec discrepancies remain: String encoding; deprecated signature and locations; interface covariance and extra arguments; skip/include argument types and support wording; anonymous operations with variables; validation reuse; query execution order and side effects; pagination examples versus connection requirements; precise data/errors result rules; nullable-variable default exceptions; null-error phase distinctions; propagation to the nearest nullable ancestor; contradictory schema-change nullability examples; and optional custom-directive prefixes. The pinned specification decides each conflict. All six internal caveats were confirmed: includeDeprecated nullability differs between section 4.2 and Appendix D; required-input rules permit defaults despite broader Non-Null prose; runtime nullable-variable null errors have conflicting descriptions; OneOf variable prose is stricter than its algorithm; extra-interface-argument prose overstates its non-null example; and implemented-interface spread prose needs the Resource/Node example's context. Cards avoid the disputed cases. Opened the versions index, pinned edition and all requested anchors, including every validation rule; release, both relevant changelogs, PR, October2021 and working draft; HTTP draft and versions; cursor connections; and these Learn pages: introduction/, schema/, queries/, mutations/, subscriptions/, validation/, execution/, response/, introspection/, best-practices/, thinking-in-graphs/, serving-over-http/, authorization/, pagination/, schema-design/, error-handling/, global-object-identification/, caching/, performance/, security/, debug-errors/, robust-applications/ and governance-versioning/ (Schema Change Management). No requested topic lost source support beyond the documented discrepancies. Schema Change Management permits removal after acceptable usage or a deadline, so the plan avoids a universal zero-usage requirement.

cards.statement: A mutation returns selected data after performing its write.
cards.explanation: A mutation combines a write with a fetch of the selected result, so its response can show the state produced by the write.

cards.statement: A service executes a document that combines an operation with a type definition.
cards.explanation: A document containing a type system definition is unsuitable for execution. The service should return a descriptive error.
cards.misconception: An operation makes a mixed executable and SDL document executable.

cards.statement: A document may contain several named operations together with fragment definitions.
cards.explanation: An executable document can package several operations and fragments in one request string.

cards.statement: A lone query with an operation directive qualifies for the `{ ... }` shorthand.
cards.explanation: Query shorthand requires a lone query with no variables, operation directives or description.
cards.misconception: A single query qualifies for shorthand even when it has an operation directive.

cards.statement: An anonymous query may declare variables when it is the document's single operation.
cards.explanation: The lone-anonymous-operation rule permits an unnamed operation when the document contains one operation, even if that operation declares variables.

cards.statement: A query and a mutation may share an operation name within one document.
cards.explanation: Operation names are unique across the document, including across different operation types.
cards.misconception: Operation names have separate namespaces for queries and mutations.

cards.statement: A service runs the first operation when a multi-operation request omits operationName.
cards.explanation: A request containing several operations needs operationName to identify one. Omitting it produces a request error.
cards.misconception: Document order chooses the operation when operationName is omitted.

cards.statement: A service collects exactly one root response name per valid subscription operation.
cards.explanation: The service collects a subscription's root selections, including fields reached through fragments, and checks that there is one root field.

cards.statement: A field named `userName` matches a selection named `username`.
cards.explanation: GraphQL treats names with different letter case as different names. A selection has to match the schema's spelling.
cards.misconception: GraphQL matches names case-insensitively.

cards.statement: GraphQL permits Unicode letters such as `é` inside a field name.
cards.explanation: Names use ASCII letters, digits and underscores; letters outside the ASCII range are invalid in a name.
cards.misconception: Unicode source text allows Unicode letters in GraphQL names.

cards.statement: Adding commas between selections preserves an operation's meaning.
cards.explanation: GraphQL treats separator commas as ignored tokens, so developers can use them for readability.

cards.statement: In the September 2025 spec, removing an operation description preserves its execution result.
cards.explanation: Executable descriptions supply documentation. Removing an operation's description leaves its result unchanged.

cards.statement: The service nests `name` inside `user` when `user { name }` produces an object result.
cards.explanation: An object's selected subfields become entries in its result object, mirroring the nesting of the selection.

cards.statement: A field needs an object return type to declare arguments.
cards.explanation: Fields returning scalars can declare arguments too, such as a picture field taking a size argument.
cards.misconception: Arguments are available solely on fields returning objects.

cards.statement: Reordering named arguments preserves the meaning of a field selection.
cards.explanation: GraphQL matches supplied arguments by name, so their order in the document has no semantic effect.

cards.statement: A client may supply an undeclared field argument when its value is a scalar.
cards.explanation: A field selection accepts the arguments defined for that field. A scalar value does not make an unknown argument valid.
cards.misconception: Any scalar-valued argument name is acceptable.

cards.statement: A repeated argument in a field selection takes its last supplied value.
cards.explanation: Repeating an argument name within one field selection is invalid; GraphQL rejects the ambiguity.
cards.misconception: Repeated argument names use a last-value-wins rule.

cards.statement: The alias in `label: name` makes `label` the response name for that result.
cards.explanation: An alias supplies the key for a selected field's value in the response object.

cards.statement: A client may choose `__label` as the alias for an ordinary field selection.
cards.explanation: The reserved prefix restricts schema names, while field aliases have no such restriction.

cards.statement: A query may select `item(id: 1)` and `item(id: 2)` under one response name on the same object type.
cards.explanation: Selections under the same parent type need identical arguments to share a response name.
cards.misconception: Selections with different arguments merge under the same response name.

cards.statement: Selections on distinct object types need matching leaf types to share a response name.
cards.explanation: Even mutually exclusive object branches have to produce the same response shape for a shared response name.

cards.statement: A service adds unselected scalar fields when it completes a selected object.
cards.explanation: The client's selections determine the data fields in the response. Completing an object does not add unselected schema fields.
cards.misconception: Selecting an object implicitly selects its scalar fields.

cards.statement: A JSON response should place a fragment's fields where its spread first contributes them.
cards.explanation: A fragment contributes fields at its spread's position, helping the response follow the client's selection order.

cards.statement: A skipped occurrence fixes a field's response order before an included occurrence.
cards.explanation: Fields excluded by directives do not count toward response ordering. The first included occurrence determines the position.
cards.misconception: Skipped selections still reserve a response-order position.

cards.statement: An operation references `fragment UserBits on User` with the syntax `...UserBits`.
cards.explanation: The spread syntax uses three dots followed by the fragment's name to incorporate its field selections.

cards.statement: The service accepts a named fragment on `String` when its selected fields return strings.
cards.explanation: Fragment type conditions target object, interface or union types. A scalar such as String is an invalid target.
cards.misconception: A fragment's type condition describes the scalar values returned by its fields.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Fragments on Object, Interface or Union Types

cards.statement: The service checks a fragment's type condition against the runtime object's concrete type.
cards.explanation: A fragment applies according to the concrete object returned for that response position.

cards.statement: An inline fragment that omits `on Type` takes its type from the enclosing selection set.
cards.explanation: An inline fragment's omitted type condition inherits the surrounding type context.

cards.statement: An operation may apply a directive to a group of fields by placing them in an inline fragment.
cards.explanation: A directive on an inline fragment applies to that fragment's grouped selection set.

cards.statement: The validator treats fragment names as unique within each operation of a document.
cards.explanation: Fragment definition names are unique across the entire document, even when different operations use the definitions.
cards.misconception: Each operation has its own namespace for fragment definitions.

cards.statement: A document's unused fragment definitions pass validation when their fields match the schema.
cards.explanation: A document containing a defined fragment that is never spread fails validation.
cards.misconception: Valid field selections make an unused fragment definition acceptable.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Fragments Must Be Used

cards.statement: A fragment spread may use a named fragment defined in another document sent to the same service.
cards.explanation: A named fragment spread refers to a fragment definition in the same document.
cards.misconception: A service retains fragment definitions for use by later request documents.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Fragment Spread Target Defined

cards.statement: A fragment may spread itself indirectly when each step follows a different object field.
cards.explanation: Fragment spread cycles invalidate the document, including cycles that pass through child fields and other fragments.
cards.misconception: Changing object fields between spreads makes recursive fragments valid.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Fragment Spreads Must Not Form Cycles

cards.statement: A spread between two interfaces is possible when an object type implements both interfaces.
cards.explanation: A shared possible object type gives the parent interface and fragment condition a nonempty intersection.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — Fragment Spread Is Possible

cards.statement: The spec treats fragments as the primary unit for composing GraphQL selections.
cards.explanation: Fragments provide the specification's main mechanism for composing field-selection components.

cards.statement: An inline fragment declares a name that later fragment spreads can reference.
cards.explanation: An inline fragment supplies its selection set at its location and declares no fragment name.
cards.misconception: Inline fragments define reusable names for later spreads.

cards.statement: Two operations in one document may each declare `$limit` with their own variable type.
cards.explanation: Variable-name uniqueness is checked per operation, so separate operations can declare the same name independently.

cards.statement: Each operation that reaches a fragment using `$limit` declares `$limit` in its variable definitions.
cards.explanation: Variable uses in transitively referenced fragments are checked against the consuming operation's variable definitions.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — All Variable Uses Defined

cards.statement: An operation may declare an unused variable when the client supplies a value for it.
cards.explanation: An unused variable definition makes an operation invalid. Supplying its value does not create a variable use.
cards.misconception: A supplied runtime value makes an unused variable declaration valid.

cards.statement: The service replaces an explicit null variable value with the variable's declared default.
cards.explanation: A variable's default applies when its value is omitted. An explicit null is a supplied value.
cards.misconception: Variable defaults replace both omitted values and explicit null.

cards.statement: A variable declared as `$size: Int = 10` is valid at an argument of type `Int!`.
cards.explanation: A non-null variable default permits this nullable variable at a non-null argument position.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — All Variable Usages Are Allowed

cards.statement: A variable of type `[Int]` is valid at an argument of type `[Int!]` when the supplied items are integers.
cards.explanation: Validation compares declared types. Nullable list items in `[Int]` are incompatible with the non-null items expected by `[Int!]`.
cards.misconception: Runtime item values override incompatible variable item nullability during validation.

source.title: GraphQL Specification — All Variable Usages Are Allowed

cards.statement: A block string turns the characters `\n` into a line break in its input value.
cards.explanation: A block string preserves `\n` as a backslash followed by `n` rather than interpreting it as an escape sequence.
cards.misconception: Block strings interpret ordinary string escape sequences.

cards.statement: The service accepts the JSON variable string `"123"` as a value for a variable of type `Int`.
cards.explanation: Int input coercion rejects strings with numeric content; `"123"` remains a string input.
cards.misconception: Int input coercion parses numeric strings into integers.

cards.statement: The service accepts the integer literal `123` as an input value for an argument of type `Float`.
cards.explanation: Float input coercion converts an accepted integer input to a floating-point value.

cards.statement: The service may accept the JSON variable string `"RED"` for an enum type that defines `RED`.
cards.explanation: JSON has no separate enum representation, so a variable string may identify the enum value with that name.

cards.statement: The service coerces the integer literal `5` to `[5]` when an argument expects `[Int]`.
cards.explanation: List input coercion wraps an accepted single item in a list of length one.

cards.statement: The service ignores extra fields supplied in an input object value after reading its defined fields.
cards.explanation: An input object value containing a field absent from its expected input type raises a request error.
cards.misconception: Input object coercion discards unknown fields like a permissive object parser.
